newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Moslem Uighurs say bombed Chinese bus "in revenge".
newsitem.headline: Moslem Uighurs say bombed Chinese bus "in revenge".

text.p: An exiled spokesman for Uighur nationalists in western China said on Tuesday his group had staged a bomb attack on a Chinese bus on Monday in reprisal for Beijing government measures against the Moslem ethnic group.

Mukhiddin Mukhlisi told Reuters in the nearby Kazakh capital Almaty he did not know how many victims there were in the attack, 120 km (75 miles) east of Yining in Xinjiang province. Chinese officials have said seven people died and over 60 were hurt in three previous bus bomb attacks in the region last week.

"The explosion in the bus near the town of Kuldji (Yining) ...was our act of revenge for the crimes of the Chinese authorities," Mukhlisi, a prominent spokesman for the Uighur nationalist cause in exile, said.
He accused the Chinese police and army of killing 127 Uighurs and arresting hundreds more in a campaign against nationalists seeking an independent homeland, which he said was launched last month.
Mukhlisi said Chinese authorities were pursuing a deliberate policy of bringing in ethnic Han Chinese immigrants to Xinjiang and giving them favourable treatment over Uighurs.
"We intend to continue our struggle, he added."

Last week's time-bombs coincided with funeral rites for Beijing's political patriarch Deng Xiaoping and were the latest example of brewing unrest in the oil-rich region, where most of China's Turkic-speaking Uighurs live.

A spokesman for Uighur exiles in Russia, Sargari Tarym, said last week in Moscow: "We think that, in general, Deng's death will bring a power struggle within the Chinese elite. If that happens, the independence movement in Turkestan will intensify."
In February a huge anti-Chinese riot by local Uighurs broke out in the north of China.

Beijing said the riot had erupted after an Uighur criminal suspect resisted arrest by police, while Uighur exile leaders said it was triggered by "China's colonial policy, genocide, mass influx of ethnic Han Chinese and social economic problems of the Uighurs".
Chinese officials said nine people had been killed in clashes with the army and the police. Uighur leaders put the figure at 80 dead at least.
The riot was one of the largest, most violent demonstrations for independence in Xinjiang since the 1949 communist takeover.
Officially some nine million Uighurs live in China but nationalists, striving for an independent "East Turkestan" homeland, put the number at over 20 million.
As many as 300,000 Uighurs live in the former Soviet Union, to which many fled in the 1960s during a period of Han Chinese discrimination against ethnic minorities.
About 180,000 have settled in what is now independent Kazakhstan, whose native Kazakhs are also of Turkic origin.
